title: FHA Loan Essentials
subtitle: A confident first conversation
scope: Introductory training for Mortgage Loan Officers on a standard FHA-insured purchase mortgage for a principal residence. Other FHA programs, detailed underwriting, and lender-specific overlays are outside this sample.

sources.name: HUD: FHA consumer factsheet
sources.use: FHA insures lender-made mortgages, low down payment, principal residence.

sources.name: HUD: Handbook 4000.1 information page
sources.use: Verify applicable policy, documentation, and effective dates.

sources.name: HUD: Mortgage insurance premium structure FAQ
sources.use: Most FHA programs have upfront MIP and annual MIP paid in monthly installments.

sources.name: HUD: 2026 FHA loan limits
sources.use: Loan limits vary by area and property units; verify the applicable case-number year.

decisions.title: The down payment question
decisions.quote: Alex says: ‘The home is $300,000 and I saved $10,500. Does that mean I have enough to close?’
decisions.context: Training assumption: adjusted value is $300,000 and the borrower is eligible for 3.5% minimum investment. No closing-cost estimate has been prepared.
choices: ‘That is 3.5% in this example. Let’s review closing costs, prepaids, funding sources, and your lender’s requirements before estimating the total.’
‘Yes. You have the 3.5% down payment, so $10,500 covers the entire transaction.’

feedback.title: Alex understands there is more to estimate.
feedback.body: You separated the illustrative minimum investment from total cash needed. Costs, eligible credits, financing choices, and the borrower’s file must be verified before quoting cash to close.
feedback.takeaway: A minimum down payment is one part of the transaction.

feedback.title: Alex now assumes no other funds are needed.
feedback.body: The minimum investment is not a complete cash-to-close figure. Your answer could leave Alex unprepared for closing costs and prepaid items.
feedback.takeaway: Explain the cost categories before giving a total.

decisions.title: The property-use question
decisions.quote: Alex says: ‘I plan to keep living where I am and rent this house out from day one.’
decisions.context: The conversation concerns a standard FHA purchase mortgage for a principal residence.
choices: ‘As long as you can make the payment, we can treat it as your primary home.’
‘Let’s document how you actually plan to use the property and confirm the appropriate program with our team.’

feedback.title: The application could misstate the intended use.
feedback.body: Ability to make the payment does not make a rental property a principal residence. Do not alter the stated purpose to fit a program.

feedback.title: The program question goes to the right review.
feedback.body: You identified a mismatch between the stated use and the standard principal-residence purchase scope. Record the facts and seek the appropriate program review without promising eligibility.
feedback.takeaway: Clarify the facts before discussing program fit.

decisions.title: A different property
decisions.quote: Alex later asks about a home they would occupy in a different county: ‘Can we use the same loan limit and payment estimate?’
decisions.context: The property and county changed. The applicable case-number year and lender review still need confirmation.
decisions.prompt: What is the best next step?
choices: ‘We need to verify the new county’s limit, property units, applicable year, and updated costs, including mortgage insurance, before confirming an estimate.’
‘Yes. FHA has one national limit, and mortgage insurance works the same for every loan.’

feedback.title: Alex gets an accurate next step.
feedback.body: You identified the items that need rechecking. FHA limits depend on location and units, while mortgage insurance details and other costs must be verified for the specific loan.
feedback.takeaway: A property change can require a new review.

feedback.title: The estimate rests on two unsupported assumptions.
feedback.body: There is no single limit for every property. Most FHA programs include upfront and annual MIP, but the applicable amount and duration require verification.
feedback.takeaway: Verify current limits and mortgage insurance details.

choices: An FHA-approved lender makes the loan; FHA provides mortgage insurance.
The county government automatically funds it.
quiz.why: FHA insures eligible mortgages made by approved lenders. It is not the lender in this transaction.

quiz.q: For an eligible borrower in this example, adjusted value is $300,000 and minimum investment is 3.5%. What is the investment?
quiz.why: $300,000 × 0.035 = $10,500. This is an illustrative minimum investment, not the total cash needed to close.

quiz.q: Alex plans to rent the home out immediately and will not live there. What should the MLO do?
choices: Document the actual intended use and seek appropriate program review.
Mark it as a principal residence so it fits the program.
Treat the down payment as proof of eligibility.
quiz.why: The sample covers a standard principal-residence FHA purchase. The intended use must be recorded accurately and reviewed for appropriate program fit.

quiz.q: Which cost explanation is most accurate for a standard FHA purchase discussion?
choices: The down payment is always the entire amount due at closing.
Discuss the down payment, other closing items, and applicable upfront and annual mortgage insurance.
Mortgage insurance can be omitted whenever the customer asks.
quiz.why: The down payment does not describe every transaction cost. Most FHA programs include upfront MIP and annual MIP collected monthly; verify amounts and duration.

quiz.q: The customer chooses a home in another county. What must you verify before confirming the limit?
choices: A limit from an old loan in another area.
The property’s county, unit count, and applicable FHA case-number year.
quiz.why: FHA limits vary by area and units and are published for applicable years. Check current HUD resources and lender requirements.
